 Source: Tennessee Gov.-elect Blackburn not choosing Hegseth to take over her Senate seat
 By Manu Raju 
 Governor-elect Sen. Marsha Blackburn speaks during a news conference in Nashville, Tennessee on Wednesday. 
 George Walker IV/AP 
 Tennessee Governor-elect Marsha Blackburn will not be choosing Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to fill her soon-to-be vacated Senate seat, a source close to her told CNN on Thursday.
 The Tennessee GOP senator defeated Democrat Jerri Green in the midterms race.
 Many Republican lawmakers and allies are pinning blame for the election results on Hegseth. The defense secretary has vowed to fight a brewing impeachment effort as President Donald Trump said he has “every intention to keep” Hegseth.

 Next mayor of Los Angeles is honored city "voted for an immigrant to be their next mayor"
 By Taylor Romine 
 Los Angeles Mayor-elect Nithya Raman speaks in Los Angeles on Thursday. 
 Jae C. Hong/AP 
 Incoming mayor of Los Angeles Nithya Raman said she is honored that Angelinos “voted for an immigrant to be their next mayor at this moment in American history.”
 “Over the past few years we’ve seen a country that has rejected immigrants, and in so many ways, they’ve been redeemed” by this mayoral race, Raman told reporters Thursday, surrounded by her staff.
 “I’m an immigrant to this country, and this is a city of immigrants in so many ways, whether they came from across America or whether they came from across the world,” she continued. “This city has opened its arms to people to come and build their dreams here. And the idea that Angelinos voted for an immigrant to be their next mayor at this moment in American history is so deeply moving to me.”
 Raman’s win comes after last year’s chaotic immigration raids , which took place in public and at workplaces, tore through the city as part of President Donald Trump’s deportation agenda .
 Raman also took the time to thank her predecessor and opponent in the race Mayor Karen Bass, saying “her decades of service” in and for the community “has made Los Angeles what it is today,” which is “a deeply, deeply inclusive place.”
 The two have spoken and are committed to a smooth transition, she said.
 Raman said she also spoke with city council members, who all supported Bass in her reelection campaign as ideological issues played out. Every call came with a congratulations and a “shared commitment to working together for the betterment of this city,” she said.
 “No matter what happened during the campaign, that is in the past now,” Raman said. She went on to say she is committed to her key priorities, which include homelessness, housing, public safety and economic development.

 Pentagon staff rally around Hegseth in social media blitz amid impeachment push
 By Haley Britzky and Alayna Treene 
 Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth leaves after testifying during a Senate Appropriations Committee hearing on Capitol Hill, on July 21. 
 Finn Gomez/Getty Images 
 Public affairs staff and advisers to Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth flooded social media on Thursday with images of Hegseth and one phrase, “Stand. Fight. Defend the Republic.”
 The campaign appears to be part of an “aggressive defense” of Hegseth ahead of an anticipated impeachment fight . Deputy Pentagon press secretary Joel Valdez said in a statement to CNN that chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell “convened the team to map the most aggressive defense of Secretary Hegseth and the President’s agenda ever assembled, paired with planned offensive maneuvers that will define the next phase.”
 “The full scope of that strategy is not being disclosed,” Valdez said.
 Posts were made by roughly a dozen civilian public affairs staff and advisers and the Pentagon’s rapid response account , as well as accounts of others who have worked or currently work in the Pentagon for Hegseth, including at least one active duty Army lieutenant colonel. The White House social media account also posted a video of Hegseth and Trump’s praise of him.
 Stand. Fight. Defend the Republic. https://t.co/fVIHpv4gdM 
— Sean Parnell (@SeanParnellASW) November 5, 2026 
 A senior administration official told CNN that “the Pentagon and White House made their positions crystal clear tonight. They are coming out swinging in support of Hegseth and that should tell you everything you need to know.”
 The social media campaign came just a couple of hours after Hegseth posted to X a defiant video on the steps of the Pentagon, criticizing the “sham” effort to impeach him by members of Congress. “At the War Department: We Stand. We Fight. We Defend the Republic,” Hegseth said in the post, referencing the Department of Defense’s secondary name.

 Asian markets slump following Wall Street sell-off
 By Stephanie Yang 
 An electronic board displays the Nikkei Stock Average (Nikkei 225) in Minato Ward, Tokyo on November 6, 2026. 
 Koji Ito/AP 
 Stock markets in Asia plunged Friday, following a tech-led sell-off in the US on anticipation that newly elected Democratic officials could stymie an AI investment boom that’s driven global stocks to record highs.
 South Korea’s Kospi index dropped more than 8% after opening, triggering a halt in trading on the exchange, while Japan’s Nikkei 225 index fell about 6%. Taiwan’s benchmark Taiex index also declined about 8% in morning trading.
 Asian tech companies, which play an integral role in the global electronics supply chain, have been buoyed by insatiable demand for components such as semiconductors needed to build massive AI data centers. Some economists estimate that AI infrastructure led by US tech giants including Nvidia could reach $1 trillion a year in the coming years.
 However, backlash against the environmental and community impact of new data centers turned AI spending into a key issue in the US midterm elections. Democrats won control of the House of Representatives and the Senate, and flipped several other contested state seats.
 That sweeping victory has spurred concerns that Democratic representatives could now block or slow spending on new AI infrastructure, stalling a key driver of economic growth for both the US and Asia.

 Democrats have won their largest majority in the house in nearly 20 years, and there’s a chance it could expand — 30 races are still yet to be called .
 They could also widen their lead in the Senate, with races in Alaska and Mississippi remaining very close.
 Meantime, Republicans are discussing what their strategy will be when the new Congress is sworn in in January.
 Here’s what else to know:
 Democrats have won more than 250 seats in the House, CNN’s Decision Desk projects . More than 30 incumbent members of Congress lost their seat. In the Senate, Democrats are projected to have already secured 54 seats .
 The Democratic candidate could have won in Senate races in Georgia, North Carolina and Texas , as well as Arizona’s governor’s race, even if literally none of their voters showed up on Election Day due to early voting and absentee and/or mail voting numbers.
 In the latest projection, Republican Paul LePage , a former governor of Maine, will win the race for the state’s 2nd District, flipping the rural seat from blue to red after his Democratic opponent, state Auditor Matt Dunlap, conceded the race today.
 White House officials, including senior staff members, held a meeting Wednesday to discuss paths forward now that Republicans have lost control of Congress, according to two sources familiar with the event. The meeting included discussion of potential executive orders and whether Democrats would be willing to work with the White House.
 Mississippi Republicans today raised the possibility of taking legal action in the still undecided Senate race where Democrat Scott Colom holds a narrow lead over GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. As many as 20,000 ballots, by Republicans’ estimates, remain uncounted. They include some absentee ballots as well as provisional ballots.
 Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said his country’s “chances of receiving additional assistance from the United States of America may now increase ” after this week’s historic blue wave.
 Looking ahead to 2028, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear said the massive win for Democratic governors, which includes five flipped seats , can be an example of the kind of candidate that should run for president.
 Meantime, a sell-off rippled through Wall Street today, wiping out roughly $2.5 trillion in market value from the Nasdaq Composite on fears that Democrats’ midterm gains could put the brakes on the AI buildout. President Donald Trump blamed the sell-off on Democrats and claimed the market would come back under his leadership.

 Mississippi GOP raises possibility of legal action in tight Senate race
 By Tierney Sneed 
 Mississippi Republicans today raised the possibility of taking legal action in the still undecided Senate race where Democrat Scott Colom holds a narrow lead over GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, promising to “fight like hell” to make sure election officials were following the law in the count of outstanding ballots.
 At a press conference in Jackson, Mississippi, state Republican Party Chair Mike Hurst said the party has deployed more than 50 volunteer attorneys and observers to ballot counting sites across the state, and that many more were ready jump in if necessary.
 “Our attorneys and observers, right now, are documenting developments, preserving facts and evidence, and recording every step of what occurred on Election Day, and what has happened since Election Day, so that we will be ready, if necessary, to avail ourselves of every legal option at our disposal if there is evidence that the law has been violated,” Hurst said.
 Colom’s lead grew to over 1,700 votes over Hyde-Smith on Thursday afternoon, but thousands of ballots – as many as 20,000, by Republicans’ estimates – remain uncounted. They include some absentee ballots, as well as provisional ballots that were cast because the voter lacked photo ID or was not showing up in their precinct’s poll book
 Hurst said Republicans were “enthusiastic” about those ballots, expressing confidence that Hyde-Smith would ultimately prevail. But he also nodded vaguely to concerns about whether election officials were following the law and said Republicans would hold them “accountable” if not.
 The National Republican Senate Committee sent election officials letters requesting that the provisional ballots be segregated and that other related records be preserved — which Hurst described as a standard legal step.
 “Let me be clear, there’s no election denying going on here,” he said. “If the laws are followed and the voters spoke, that is it.”
 A lawyer representing Colom’s campaign urged election officials in a letter on Thursday to deny the request, arguing that segregating the ballots would violate state election law.
 CNN’s Annie Grayer contributed to this post.

 Here is how Texas' incoming governor says she plans to approach data centers
 By Taylor Romine 
 In an aerial view, sections of the Stargate Oracle AI data center undergoe construction in Abilene, Texas, on August 26 
 Brandon Bell/Getty Images 
 Democrat Gina Hinojosa shared her vision for how Texas will approach data centers after her projected victory in the gubernatorial race, telling CNN she will focus on partnership and community control while emphasizing the state still cares about business.
 “We have always been a pro-business state in Texas,” Hinojosa told CNN’s Jake Tapper. “But what changes now with me as governor is it has to be a partnership that benefits Texans. And right now, what has happened is data centers have moved into mostly rural communities, and there are no rules and laws to protect Texans, and Texans are being taken advantage of.”
 Instead, those communities need to have a seat at the table to decide if and how data centers can be built, she said.
 “So the difference is we will have laws to protect Texans, and we need to stop what we are doing with data centers until we have those protections,” she said. “We can have a strong economy, strong industry and protections for the people of Texas. Those things are not mutually exclusive.”
 The topic is especially top of mind today as a massive market sell-off wiped out about $2.5 trillion in market value from the Nasdaq Composite after fears that Democratic wins could potentially pause AI growth. Texas has played a crucial role in accelerating AI advancements, with top tech companies making massive investments in data centers there.

 Trump blames Democrats for tumbling stocks after midterms
 By Alejandra Jaramillo 
 President Donald Trump blamed Democrats for today’s steep stock market sell-off that followed the party’s gains in the midterm elections.
 “The Stock Market suffered one of the Worst Days in History based on the results of the Election,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post. “Such a sad thing to watch! It took so much work to get us to a level that no one has ever seen before, and then this. Your 401(k)s have, therefore, dropped,” he added.
 The president claimed the market would come back under his leadership.
 “Remember, it wasn’t Republicans, it was Dumocrats. Do not fear, however, we will soon, one way or the other, be BIGGER AND STRONGER THAN EVER BEFORE,” Trump wrote.
 The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell 5.52% Thursday as investors weigh whether Democrats’ midterm wins could slow the huge data center buildout behind the tech industry’s growth, which has helped drive the broader US economy.
 The Nasdaq ended the day in correction territory, more than 10% below its October 6 record high.
 The sell-off reached the broader market as well. The S&P 500 and the Dow also had their worst days since April 2025.

 Republican former Gov. Paul LePage will flip Maine’s 2nd District after Democratic concession
 By Kathryn Squyres and Ethan Cohen 
 Former Maine Gov. Paul LePage greets supporters in Brewer Maine, during a rally with Vice President JD Vance on August 24. 
 Gabe Souza/AP 
 Republican Paul LePage, a former governor of Maine, will win the race for the state’s 2nd District, flipping the rural seat from blue to red after his Democratic opponent, state Auditor Matt Dunlap, conceded the race Thursday.
 The Maine Secretary of State announced Thursday that the race would proceed to a ranked choice tabulation but given LePage leads by about 5,400 votes and there are only about 6,100 write-in and blank ballots that could potentially be reallocated, Dunlap’s odds of overtaking LePage are vanishingly small.
“This isn’t the result we were hoping for, and I’m disappointed that we came short,” Dunlap said in a statement.
 LePage will succeed Democratic Rep. Jared Golden, whose decision to not seek reelection opened up the race for Republicans in a competitive district.

 Some Democrats would have won their Senate races even without any Election Day votes
 By Aaron Blake and Dianne Gallagher 
 Jon Ossoff addresses the crowd at his election night watch party in Atlanta, on Tuesday. 
 Audra Melton for CNN 
 How dominant were Democrats in the 2026 election?
 So dominant that they could have won some marquee races even if literally none of their voters showed up on Election Day.
 That was true in Senate races in Georgia, North Carolina and Texas. And it could also be true of the Arizona governor’s race.
 In each one, more voters voted for the Democrat via early voting and absentee and/or mail voting than voted in total for the Republican — including all methods of voting. In each race, the Democrat appears to have won by 10 or more percentage points.
 In Georgia, returns from the secretary of state show Sen. Jon Ossoff getting about 1,772,000 votes from early and absentee voting, compared to about 1,712,000 total votes for his opponent, GOP Rep. Mike Collins.
 Ossoff’s current lead stands at 18 points.
 In North Carolina, data from the State Board of Elections shows Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper receiving about 1,728,000 early in-person votes, compared to about 1,643,000 votes total for Republican Michael Whatley.
 Cooper didn’t even need absentee votes to beat Whatley. His early vote total trumped Whatley’s total from early, absentee and Election Day voting.President Donald Trump came to the state repeatedly to try to help Whatley, and Cooper is currently winning by 20 points. He is the first Democrat North Carolina has elected to the Senate since 2008.
 The stats reinforce just how crucial the early vote is to Democrats, in particular. Democratic voters remained significantly more likely to vote early than Republicans in these midterms.

 Punishing market sell-off tied to fears Democrats’ gains could put brakes on AI buildout
 By Elisabeth Buchwald , John Towfighi and Matt Egan 
 Televisions broadcast market news at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York, Thursday. 
 Michael Nagle/Bloomberg/Getty Images 
 A punishing sell-off rippled through Wall Street on Thursday, wiping out roughly $2.5 trillion in market value from the Nasdaq Composite on fears that Democrats’ midterm gains could put the brakes on the AI buildout.
 The Nasdaq slumped 5.52% and closed in correction, trading down more than 10% from its record high on October 6.
 The tech-heavy index suffered its worst day since April 2025, when President Donald Trump unveiled sweeping global tariffs. Thursday’s sell-off extended to broader indexes, with the S&P 500 and the Dow both posting their worst day since April 2025.
 It’s a sharp reversal from Wednesday’s historic post-midterm rally , when the Dow soared 1,569 points and the Nasdaq rose 1.44%. By Thursday the Dow closed 1,833 points lower, wiping out all of those gains.
 While the major indexes rose Wednesday, underneath the surface, shares of semiconductor chipmakers and companies involved in the AI data center buildout were falling. That selling pressure intensified on Thursday, dragging the indexes down sharply.
 Key to the sell-off is Texas’ gubernatorial Democratic victory, given the state has played a crucial role in accelerating AI advancements, with the likes of Google, Meta, Oracle and OpenAI making massive investments in data centers there. Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned on a temporary data center moratorium and eliminating certain tax incentives for businesses building data centers in the state.

 Sources: White House aides met to discuss path forward after losing Congress 
 2:02
 White House officials, including senior staff members, held a meeting Wednesday to discuss paths forward now that Republicans have lost control of Congress, according to two sources familiar with the event.
 President Donald Trump did not attend.
 The meeting covered a wide range of topics, including discussion of potential executive orders, whether Democrats would be willing to work with the White House and potential issues they could collaborate on in a divided government.
 Officials also discussed a scenario in which Democrats immediately launch into expansive investigations, which the White House would meet with a much more aggressive posture, the sources said.
 While administration officials knew that losing both the House and Senate was a possibility, officials were shocked at the extent of the GOP’s defeat Tuesday night . Much of the conversation around divided government before the midterms were based on predictions that, whoever won control of Congress, it would only be by narrow margins.
 Democrats holding more than 250 seats in the House, as CNN has projected, has changed some of White House officials’ calculus on those preliminary plans.

 By Taylor Romine 
 Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear waves as he takes the stage to campaign for Democratic candidates in Council Bluffs, Iowa, on Sunday. 
 Ellen Schmidt/AP 
 The massive win for Democratic governors, which includes 5 flipped seats , can be an example of the kind of candidate that should run for president in 2028, said Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, who is also the chair of the Democratic Governors Association.
 If the next Democratic nominee is smart, they will “lean on these governors who have shown us the way, who know how to win in their states and who could help elect the next Democratic president,” Beshear told CNN’s Kasie Hunt.
 Part of the winning strategy should be considering what made Democrats appealing in more red or purple states, he added.
 “The right candidate is one that’s not overly focused on ideology but is practical, recognizes that the American people are suffering,” he said. “The right candidate is one that spends 80% of his or her time focused on things that matter to 100% of the American people.”
 A Democratic governor would be uniquely qualified to tackle this role, he said.
 Beshear, a Democratic governor in a traditionally red state who has considered running for president , told Hunt he is still considering the choice and will contemplate it more seriously once things slow down after the midterms.

 “I voted for Bruce and straight Republican ticket and have worked for decades helping Republicans across the state and country including him,” she continued. “We will need everyone to be a constructive part of the effort to rebuild Republican support as we learn from this historic loss.”

 Midterm voters look ahead to 2028 election
 With the midterm elections over, Democrats and Republicans are already considering who they want to see on the ballot in the 2028 presidential election. CNN reporters asked midterm voters at polling locations around the country who they would pick in two years.

 Midterm voters look ahead to 2028 election 
 1:48
 Democrats have won more than 250 seats in the House, CNN’s Decision Desk projects , their largest majority since 2008. There are more than 30 races yet to be called, which means the party could have its largest majority since the early 1990s .
 In the Senate, Democrats are projected to have already secured 54 seats . Whether that total could expand to 55 or even 56 seats depends on two Senate races — in Alaska and Mississippi — that are both extraordinarily close.
 As both parties await the final tallies, Democrats are celebrating and beginning to discuss their plans for when they take control of Congress in January. The GOP is digesting its grim results, and a primary target of blame is emerging: the war in Iran.
 Get up to speed on all the latest developments: 
 New LA mayor: The second-largest city in the country will soon join New York in being led by a democratic socialist after city councilmember Nithya Raman defeated incumbent Karen Bass in the Los Angeles mayoral election, CNN projects.
 Positive signs for Mississippi Dems: After leading by just 67 votes after Election Night, Democratic candidate Scott Colom’s margin in the Senate race has grown to over 1,700 votes . Colom told CNN he is confident about his chances of winning because provisional ballots tend to favor Democrats. But it could take until next week , at least, for more clarity on those ballots and the race at large.
 Sullivan, Peltola in tight contest: The Alaska Senate race is neck and neck with about 74% of the vote counted. An analysis shows that incumbent GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan could gain thousands of votes if the race goes to its ranked-choice tabulations. The question is whether that will be enough to make up his deficit to Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola, which could grow as the final quarter of the vote is counted.
 Republican fallout: Members of the GOP are casting blame in all directions for their historically poor midterm performance. Many are turning against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth for his part in the unpopular Iran war, to which Vice President JD Vance and others have attributed the midterm outcome. Trump said he fields calls from people unhappy with Hegseth but isn’t planning to get rid of him.
 Implications for Supreme Court: Republicans are also feeling uneasy about the future of the Supreme Court given Democrats’ impending majorities and reported decisions by Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas to not step down.
 Newsom pardons death row: Meanwhile, California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a potential presidential contender for Democrats in 2028, is commuting the sentence of every death row prisoner in the state to a sentence of life in prison without parole.
